question: In a typical twin jet, where are the generator feeder cables routed to?

options.text: Directly to each flight deck circuit breaker panel in turn
To a separate bus bar in each wing tip
Straight to the batteries in the tail
A central distribution compartment

explanation: Feeders from each engine and the APU run through the wings and fuselage to a central compartment, usually below the flight deck or cabin floor.

question: Which items would be found in the main distribution compartment?

options.text: The RAT and its deployment actuator, with the APU
GCBs, BTBs, GCUs and main bus bars
Engine starters and igniters
Fuel pumps and hydraulic reservoirs

explanation: The compartment houses GCBs, BTBs, GCUs or regulators, current transformers, main buses and their protection, and the battery and charger.

question: Where may bus bar extensions be found on the flight deck?

options.text: Under the pilots' seats
Inside the control column and rudder pedal boxes
Behind the circuit breaker panels
Inside the instrument panel lights

explanation: Bus bars and their extensions are found behind the rear, side and overhead circuit breaker panels.

question: Are the alternators in a split bus system designed to run in parallel?

options.text: No
Yes, always
Only during autoland, when two supplies are joined
Only above 10 000 ft

explanation: Split bus alternators are not paralleled, so no complex paralleling and load sharing circuits are needed.

question: How is 28 V DC obtained in the split bus system described?

options.text: The battery charger alone, from the battery bus
A static inverter on each bus
Two TRUs fed from the two AC buses
Two DC generators on the engines

explanation: Two transformer rectifier units convert 115 V AC from the two separate AC buses to 28 V DC.

question: What can the battery in a split bus aircraft be used for?

options.text: Starting the main engines directly
Paralleling the two generators together
Supplying all AC loads for several hours after a failure
Starting the APU and limited emergency power

explanation: The battery starts the APU, supplies limited emergency power to essential buses, and can supply air and electrics on the ground with the engine generators off.

question: In a split bus system, one alternator fails. What happens?

options.text: The BTB closes; one alternator feeds both
The static inverter feeds both main buses
All non-essential loads are lost at once
Both main buses are isolated until landing

explanation: The BTB joins the main buses into one, so power to all buses is maintained; the APU can then be started to restore full power.

question: After one alternator fails in a split bus system, how can full power be restored?

options.text: Switch on the emergency static inverter
Start the APU and connect its generator to a bus
Reconnect the failed generator's drive in flight
Parallel the two buses permanently through the TRUs

explanation: The APU can be started in flight and its generator connected to AC bus 1 or 2.

question: In the split bus system described, what normally supplies the essential AC bus?

options.text: Both main buses in parallel
The static inverter at all times
The APU generator only, even in normal flight
No. 1 main bus, through a changeover relay

explanation: Each alternator feeds its own non-essential services and TRU, but the essential AC bus is normally fed from No. 1 main bus via a changeover relay.

question: Normally, how are the main AC buses of a split bus system connected to each other?

options.text: Tied through the synchronising bus
They are isolated from each other
Permanently tied together
Tied through the TRUs

explanation: The main AC buses are normally isolated, so the alternators are not paralleled; the BTB only closes after a failure.

question: Both alternators fail in a split bus system. What supplies the essential AC bus?

options.text: The galley bus, through a changeover relay
The TRUs
The emergency static inverter
The non-essential AC bus

explanation: Non-essential AC is isolated and the changeover relay connects the essential AC bus to the emergency static inverter.

question: For how long should the static inverter supply the essential AC buses after both alternators fail?

options.text: 30 minutes, with charged batteries
5 minutes, whatever the battery state
Until landing, however long that takes
3 hours, with fully charged batteries

explanation: With batteries fully charged, the emergency static inverter should supply the essential AC buses for 30 minutes.

subtopic: DC in a split bus system
question: In the split bus system described, what do the two TRUs supply?

options.text: No. 1 essential DC; No. 2 non-essential DC
Both feed only the AC essential bus
Both feed only the battery bus
No. 1 non-essential DC; No. 2 the hot battery bus

explanation: No. 1 TRU supplies essential DC loads and No. 2 TRU supplies non-essential DC loads.

subtopic: DC in a split bus system
question: What normally joins the essential and non-essential DC buses?

options.text: The bus tie breaker
The generator circuit breaker
The emergency static inverter
The DC isolation relay

explanation: In normal operation the two DC buses are connected by the isolation relay.

subtopic: DC in a split bus system
question: How are the batteries connected in the split bus system described?

options.text: Only through the TRUs
To the battery bus; via a relay to essential DC
Only to the non-essential DC bus
Directly to both main AC buses

explanation: The batteries feed the battery bus directly and the essential DC bus through the battery relay.

subtopic: DC in a split bus system
question: One alternator fails in the split bus system. What happens to the DC supply?

options.text: Only essential DC is kept
The batteries take over all DC loads
Both TRUs stay powered, so all DC remains
All DC is lost until the APU starts

explanation: With the BTB closed, both TRUs are still supplied and continue to feed all DC consumers.

subtopic: DC in a split bus system
question: Both alternators fail. What does the DC isolation relay do?

options.text: Opens, splitting essential and non-essential
Closes, joining all DC buses to the battery
Connects the static inverter to the DC buses
Connects the TRUs to the battery

explanation: The isolation relay opens; non-essential DC loses power while essential DC and AC loads are fed from the battery bus (AC via the static inverter).

subtopic: DC in a split bus system
question: How much of the system can the APU generator supply?

options.text: None; it is for starting only
All buses at all times, ground or air
Only the DC buses, through the TRUs
All on the ground; maybe one bus in flight

explanation: External power or the APU can feed all services on the ground, but the APU generator may only be able to supply one bus in flight.

question: In a parallel system, what must happen before a GCB can close?

options.text: The BTB must be opened
Output must be within limits
The battery must be disconnected
The APU must be shut down first

explanation: Operation starts with exciting the field, which brings the output within limits; only then can the GCB close.

question: Once a GCB has closed, what is its normal state?

options.text: It opens and closes with every load change
It opens after one minute
It remains closed in normal operation
It closes only during takeoff and landing

explanation: Once closed, the GCB stays closed during all normal circuit functioning.

question: In the four-generator parallel system, why does closing a GCB connect the alternator to the synchronising bus?

options.text: The BTBs are normally closed
The GCB feeds the synchronising bus directly
The SSB is always open
The BTBs are normally open

explanation: With BTBs normally closed, the load bus is already tied to the synchronising bus, so closing the GCB parallels the alternator.

question: When may a second alternator of a pair join the synchronising bus?

options.text: As soon as its engine is started
When voltage, frequency and sequence match
Whenever the first alternator is overloaded
Only after the SSB has opened

explanation: Its GCB closes only once voltage, frequency and phase sequence conditions are met.

question: What does the split system breaker (SSB) do?

options.text: Disconnects the generator drive
Joins a generator to its load bus
Joins the battery to the essential bus
Joins or splits the synchronising buses

explanation: The SSB combines or isolates the two synchronising buses depending on flight phase or system needs.

question: Why might the synchronising buses be kept separate during a dual-autopilot autoland?

options.text: To reduce the reactive load on the RAT
To let the APU take over all loads
To give each autopilot its own supply
To increase the frequency of the supply

explanation: Isolating the synchronising buses runs the alternators as two independent pairs, so a single fault cannot affect both autopilots' power.

question: One alternator fails in a paired system with the SSB open. What is the drawback?

options.text: The battery must supply that side
Both buses on that side are lost
Its partner carries a double share
The other pair is disconnected

explanation: Opening the failed alternator's GCB lets its partner carry both loads, which is more than each alternator of the other pair carries.

question: After one alternator of a pair fails, what does closing the SSB achieve?

options.text: The APU is paralleled with the engines
The failed alternator is restarted
The battery is connected to the synchronising bus
The three remaining share the load

explanation: Closing the SSB parallels the three serviceable alternators, sharing the total aircraft load.

question: There is an earth fault on a load bus. Why is opening its GCB alone not enough?

options.text: The others would feed the fault via the BTB
The GCB cannot open with an earth fault
The fault would clear itself after opening
The battery would feed the fault directly, bypassing it

explanation: With its BTB still closed, the paralleled alternators would keep feeding the fault through the synchronising bus.

question: How is an earth fault on a load bus isolated in a parallel system?

options.text: Close its BTB, then open the SSB
Open its BTB, then its GCB
Open the SSB only
Open all GCBs at once

explanation: Opening the faulty bus's BTB protects the serviceable alternators; opening the GCB of the alternator feeding it then isolates the fault completely.

question: Which aircraft type is an example of a four-generator paralleled system?

options.text: The Boeing 747-400
A twin with a split bus system
An aircraft with frequency wild generators only
A typical light single-engine trainer

explanation: The 747-400 uses four paralleled generators with split system breakers; most modern twins use split bus systems.

question: In a split bus twin, which display commonly shows the electrical system?

options.text: The weather radar display
An electronic systems display page
The standby compass card
A dedicated analogue panel only

explanation: Modern aircraft show the electrical system on electronic display pages such as ECAM or EICAS, alongside the overhead control panel.
